The amendments to the Speech from the Throne on October 18, as it appears at page 238 of Hansard, and the question which was decided by the House then, of a much more broader nature, not the precise, specific provision of home mortgage interest deductibility and/or taxation as outlined in the amendment proposed by the hon. member for York-Simcoe. The citation says that you cannot put a question more than once, and if we had that precise question in either amendment, then perhaps the matter would never have come before you, sir. Because I do not think that either the House leader or the table officers would have proposed the specific deductibility feature which is only a piece of a more substantive motion that is much more general.
Of course, as my hon. friend from Edmonton West just mentioned, there is a broader interpretation given to amendments to the Speech from the Throne or to the budget than to a specific issue which has been decided upon in the House. For those two reasons, and without getting into all the forms and precedents of Beauchesne or Standing Orders, I use your own words, sir, to put my point across, namely that if you cut a piece out of the amendment and you still have a substantive amendment, then you have not had this House decide the issue, which was used only as an example in both substantive motions and not per se the substantive motion.

Mr. Speaker, I know that it is customary wherever possible on Fridays to launch into sparkling and scintillating debate on procedure, and that you, sir, are waiting to hear other members. The hon. member for Northumberland-Miramichi (Mr. Dionne) was laughing a moment ago. I think it is a great tribute to the enduring characteristics of hon. members on the other side that they can still laugh after last night.
That is my only contribution to the budget debate, and I will now deal with the procedural issue. The Chair is probably seeking advice from hon. members because the general principle is that the Chair must always seek diligently for ways to find motions in order. That rule is particularly applicable when looking at the many traditional amendments moved in debates on the Speech from the Throne or debates on the budget.
After some soul searching 1 decided to vote for the amendment moved in the Speech from the Throne debate and which has been referred to by the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton. At that time I looked at the wording and saw that it dealt with home mortgage interest and property tax deductibility. Those are specific words that have an interpretation which falls squarely within your knowledge, sir, and mine.
I am not going to traverse the ground already covered by my colleagues on this. They have dealt adequately with it and I imagine Your Honour is prepared to find a way which would give effect to their arguments.
I would simply put this additional argument. In the motion in question appear the words "a genuine economic stimulus such as mortgage interest" which go far beyond the question of home mortgage interest. This could include mortgage interest on an industrial property or on a number of things. I submit there is a very considerable difference between "home mortgage interest" and "mortgage interest".
I do not know what I am going to do on this amendment. I still have to make up my mind.
Oh, oh!
Mr. Speaker, I hear some raucous amusement from hon. members opposite. I am simply delighted that my friends opposite can laugh today.
A point of order, Mr. Speaker. The hon. member usually has an open mind. This is the first time I have heard he has an empty mind on a subject.

Well, Mr. Speaker, unlike my hon. friend I do have a mind. To go back to where I was before I was so rudely interrupted, there is a substantial distinction between home mortgage interest and mortgage interest. We all know what a home is and mortgage interest on a home is very distinct. Home mortgage interest, as I see it, could include mortgage interest on any type of property. It may well be, as the debate develops, that colleagues on this side of the House may refine that distinction, but I see the motion at this time coming down
November 17, 1978

to a very common sense use of those words. I think I am in a lot different position in coming to a decision on this than I would have been at the time of the first motion.
I should like to go on to the second aspect. On October 18, on page 238 of Hansard, there appear the words dealing with the deductibility- "property tax deductibility". Here we have municipal tax deductibility. That is a very plain distinction. Property tax deductibility may have connotations far beyond that of municipal tax deductibility. I suggest to Your Honour, without trying to force the Chair to reach for meanings, that given the general principle that you must seek diligently, and within the limits of discretion, of course, to find ways and means to make the motion one which can be put to the House so that there can be a debate, surely Your Honour can take into account the plain distinctions that can be made in respect of the words used on October 18 and the words used today.
Those are the general arguments advanced by my colleagues. I submit there is an irresistible case made for allowing this amendment to be put.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on this particular point, the objective of our parliamentary procedure is to prevent the House of Commons from making conflicting decisions during the same session. If we compare the amendment suggested by the Progressive Conservative party to the main motion during the throne speech debate, and their amendment motion to the budget moved today, we realize that in both cases a major part of the motion is similar. Of course, I do not want to join in the acrobatics attempted by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin). A mortgage always applies to a building, but he is attempting to distinguish between a mortage on private property and a mortgage on something else. This is irrelevant because mortgages are always on buildings in any case.
I believe it was the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) who said: "Mr. Speaker, it is not because four or five words in the two motions are somewhat similar that you can conclude that these are motions of the same nature as described in citation 200 of Beauchesne on page 171". I believe that there lies the whole problem. You must answer the following question: Is it indeed a motion of the same nature as that which was moved during the throne speech debate? I recognize that it is not an easy question to answer.
In my opinion, what we must do is determine whether the motions are similar in part or whether the similar part in the two motions are in both cases major elements of the motions, which would mean that in principle, if the House were to agree to this motion today, its decision would be in conflict with that which it made during the throne speech debate. This is the question that you must answer, Mr. Speaker. The issue is not to determine whether both motions are identical from all aspects, but to see whether the similar parts are of such importance that, as a result, the House of Commons would risk in principle making two contradictory decisions within one
The Budget-Mr. Saltsman
month or five weeks of each other, or at least during the same session.
This is what Beauchesne wants to avoid by enunciating the principle that a question once made and carried in the affirmative or negative cannot be questioned again but must stand as the judgment of the House. That is a sacred rule and I think there is a very simple solution. If you have any doubt, it is because you fear that the House might indeed make a contradictory decision. Then it would be so simple if this part of the motion is not important to the Progressive Conservative party to put forward another motion through another speaker which would not include this question of mortgage interests and property tax deductibility, which was disposed of by the House very clearly during the throne speech debate.

Mr. Speaker, as must be obvious, I have been reluctant to take part in this procedural debate for the reason that we voted against the amendment the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Cros-bie) moved on October 18 and which was voted on on October 30. It might seem, therefore, that we have a conflict of interest here. Since we did not like the amendment that was moved on that occasion, it would follow we are not exactly happy with the motion before us now; but I want to make it clear that we will not shy away from expressing our views on it or from voting on it if Your Honour puts it to the House.
Your Honour interrupted my hon. friend, the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman), as he was about to move our subamendment. Without upstaging him, I can say that our subamendment was drafted as though the amendment of the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) was in order and it touches on that in that sense. In the intervening time, however, I have done some redrafting so that, if the original amendment has to be changed, our subamendment will be changed.
I want also to say that in view of these considerations I am not going to press Your Honour with all the vigour one can command in procedural debate; I do not think the world hangs on this issue. But in view of the positions that have been taken by members of the Progressive Conservative party, I feel someone in the opposition should support the position that the Chair has taken.
My friends to my right seem to be making a good deal out of the fact that the part in today's amendment that Your Honour does not like, is like the part in the amendment of October 18, and that since they are just incidental or ancillary bits in both cases, you should not be worried about them. It seems to me to work the other way. When this House on October 30 defeated the amendment moved on October 18, it did not defeat just part of it but all of it. Indeed, if there were three or four parts to that amendment and if it is possible today for the official opposition to revive one of those parts and get another vote on it, then as we move on through the session it can revive the other parts. Indeed, if we can revive this one today, we can revive it again. Therefore, a coach and

November 17, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Saltsman
four has been driven through the rule Your Honour has cited about it not being proper to seek again in the same session a decision on a motion or question on which a decision has already been taken.
My hon. friend the parliamentary secretary to the government House leader seems to approach this matter with concern lest the House reverse its position. I would say in terms of its rules the House is breaking the rules even if it takes the same decision over and over again. In my view, we should not be doing that. It seems to me the question that you raised, Mr. Speaker, is a legitimate one. I do not doubt the desire of my friends in the Progressive Conservative party to raise this issue of mortgage interest and municipal tax deductibility just as often as they can during the course of this session, but surely the rules should be observed. Although, as I say, I do not make it the case of the century, and we are not concerned, we are ready to move our subamendment either way. I hope you will stand by the view Your Honour expressed when you first raised this issue.
While I am on my feet, I must say that I have always enjoyed the contributions of my friend from Peace River (Mr. Baldwin). We have had a good time together through the years we have been here. But I did get a smile or two out of his attempt today-talk about Your Honour reaching for some way to find this matter in order, but my friend from Peace River was reaching-to try to find a difference between home mortgage interest and mortgage interest. If he is arguing today that deductibility from mortgage interest is broader than home mortgage interest, does he mean that his motion calls for all the big companies in the country that have big buildings or properties or what have you to get deductibility for those mortgages?
They already have.
You did that.
You have already given them that.

And my friend is asking for more than that. I thought my friends were concerned about the homeowners, these "poor" people who own homes. But now my friend from Peace River is not quite sure. In fact, he may not be able to vote for this. He said he had not made up his mind yet, because it refers to mortgage interest; not just home mortgage interest, but mortgage interest in the widest possible sense.
You voted on this.

We voted against the amendment that was made on October 18, and my friend knows it.
Then my friend from Peace River really stretches the point when he tries to see a difference between the phrase "property tax deductibility" and "municipal tax deductibility". Well, it is a different word. I do not know what happens to it in French;

we do not have the French translation of this day's motion yet. But really that stretches it.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that when the House voted on October 30 on the motion moved on October 18, it voted against a request for home mortgage interest and property tax deductibility. But when the Progressive Conservatives are asking us to vote today on a request for mortgage interest and municipal tax deductibility, they are asking us to vote on something on which the House has already made a decision. As I have said, we are ready to submit our amendment, to fit whatever motion comes from the Chair. But I suggest to Your Honour that your original statement was correct.
That is a rigid socialist mentality.

Mr. Speaker, I will be brief. However, I do want to point out in deference to my knowledgeable colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), that there is in fact a great deal of difference between municipal tax deductibility and property tax deductibility. I do not know precisely how all the other provinces are organized, but I know that in New Brunswick the province itself levies property tax against homeowners and there are thousands of homeowners in New Brunswick who do not live within municipalities. I would like to know what the Tories are aiming at, whether it is municipal tax deductibility or property tax deductibility. Or are they, as they usually do, trying to fudge the issue so that they can take two different positions, or four if necessary?
The same, of course, applies to home mortgage interest and mortgage interest deductibility; the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) has tried to make a difference there. He is right in the first instance but I am not so sure that he is right in the second, unless he is going to make all kinds of mortgage payments and so on deductible. It seems to me that in bragging about the brain he has he has been too clever by half. I believe he has hoisted his party upon the horns of a huge dilemma that they are now going to have trouble crawling down from unless, Mr. Speaker, you rule the motion out of order and take them down from the horns of their own dilemma.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I wish to thank hon. members for their advice and contribution to this debate. Some hon. members use such different arguments that I find it hard to come back to my own decision. The last remark made by the hon. member for Northumberland-Miramichi (Mr. Dionne), along with remarks made by the hon. member for Annapolis Valley (Mr. Nowlan) and the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), in trying to help convince me as to an analogy or a difference between two propositions is not clear to my mind. They do not take away the doubt I have.
I have forgotten which hon. member it was who said if five or six words could be taken out of the motion that would be enough to prove that they do not represent the main proposition and are secondary to the motion. This I can go along with. And I agree that the question proposed in the motion and in
November 17, 1978

the debate was broader than the one we have in front of us at this time. I agree it was twofold. As mentioned by one hon. member, on the one hand it suggested that the economy had been severely damaged; on the other, it blamed the government for not proposing some measures for tax relief. In the end, that motion, although it was twofold, singled out only one solution-among others I agree-to achieve its objective.
I do not disagree with the point raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) that it was the old motion voted upon. I wonder what the situation would be if the motion had been adopted. What if another motion or a motion to abolish property tax deductibility or a return of interest on mortgages was made? To my mind it is the duty of the Chair to protect the House and to make sure that the workings and the decisions of the House are orderly. I would like to suggest to the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) that the mere fact of speaking to the incumbent of the Chair or to a clerk at the table is not enough to obtain an absolute guarantee that a motion or a position can be acceptable. The Table is there to advise members. When I am not in the chair I do not have full power of decision. I do not have all the elements. It is when I occupy the position of Mr. Speaker that I exercise that authority.
To my mind, the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council brought out the specific point that is contrary to citation 200 of Beauchesne which states that a question having been made and carried once, it cannot be questioned again in the course of the same session.
The fact remains that I harbour a very clear and specific doubt in my mind in allowing the House to vote again. In putting before the House the proposed amendment of the official opposition, I thereby put to it part of a question which was debated and voted upon at the opening of this session. [English]
It still seems to me that by putting forward for debate the proposition of the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens), I would be putting one of the questions that was voted upon in the debate on the Speech from the Throne and upon which the House has already pronounced itself. There could be other means available to hon. members, but I will not fall into the trap of accepting the invitation of the hon. member to discuss the specifics of the motion before the House in that proposed amendment or try to indicate the exact words that could be embodied in the new proposition in relation to mortgage interest and municipal tax deductibility and try to argue the case with the hon. member as to whether or not there is a difference between those words and those contained in the motion of the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie).
I am looking through the notes I took while hon. members were so eloquently trying to convince me one way or the other and I am not sure I have covered everything, but the same
The Budget-Mr. Saltsman
doubt that struck me at the beginning is still on my mind. I did make a suggestion earlier. Is the hon. member for York-Simcoe rising on that alternative solution to the dilemma?

Mr. Speaker, I can well understand your doubt, as you express it. But I feel we must not delay a budgetary debate. In consultation with the seconder of the original motion, I suggest a revised wording of the motion. The wording I should like to suggest is:
That this House rejects a budget which increases the deficit without providing a genuine economic stimulus such as would follow from meaningful personal income tax reductions, and condemns the continued acquisition of private corporations by the government and the government's general policies ?s evidenced in the budget which continue stagnation instead of beginning the structural reforms needed for the 1980s.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
There is one thing I want to say. The rules do not allow an hon. member to amend his own motion. That rule can be found in citation 204 of Beauchesne. No member may amend his own motion, but with the leave of the House he may withdraw it and substitute another. The motion proposed by the hon. member was not put to the House. I have tried to look into the precedents taking account of the fact that I did not put the motion. If it had been put, I could not modify it without the consent of the mover, the seconder and the House. The Chair did decline to put the motion on the basis that the amendment might have been out of order.
To make it easier, taking into account the fact that some advice was sought as to its acceptability and that the main substance of the motion is definitely acceptable, I wonder whether there might not be consent, so as to simplify the problem and find a quick solution, to allow the hon. members, without further discussion, to move his amendment.
Is there consent that the hon. member be allowed to substitute an amended proposition?
Agreed.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Then I will put the modified motion to the House.
The hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman) will now resume his speech.

After such a long period of time, Mr. Speaker, it is going to be a little difficult for me to remember what I was about to move. If I might be permitted, I would say to Your Honour that this is one time when procedure and logic go together. We had the same reservations about the amendment which the hon. member for York-Simcoe offered as you did, and my hon. friend with great prescience framed a motion originally to strike out all those words as though he knew they were offensive both to procedure and equality in tax administration.
Therefore, I should like to move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That the amendment be amended by deleting all the words after the words "such as", and by substituting therefor the following words:
"the implementation of a program of public investment in housing, upgrading
of railways, urban transit and provincial-municipal capital works, and this

November 17, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Saltsman
House condemns the government for carrying out a policy of deliberately high
unemployment and for failing to reduce personal income taxes on middle and
lower-income earners. "
I find that despite the changes in the new motion moved by the hon. member for York-Simcoe, it is just as unacceptable as the old.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am very hesitant about this and I would be prepared to hear arguments from hon. members. My first impression is that the subamendment proposed tends to modify the first proposition completely. Unless it is worded in such a way as to add words to the proposition, I wonder how far we can go toward accepting subamendments which go beyond the scope of the proposition which is before us.

Mr. Speaker, if this motion is in order, it is somewhat accidentally in order. I therefore ask the indulgence of the Chair, in view of recent events surrounding this motion. It seems to me that what we are doing in our subamendment is clarifying and being very much more specific, but nevertheless along the same lines as the amendment itself. The amendment of the hon. member for York-Simcoe talks about meaningful changes. We are being very specific in terms of the use of the vague word "meaningful"; we are specifying reduced personal income taxes for middle and low income earners.

Mr. Speaker, I rise in support of the rather quick decision you have indicated. I think in drafting the proposed amendment to my motion the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) was a little too sweeping. The fact that this is the case was demonstrated when the mover of the subamendment commented that almost regardless of the final wording of our amendment his amendment would fit all right. In effect, what he was saying was that provided the New Democartic Party could tack on anything it liked after "such as", the New Democratic Party apparently felt it had a free rein to amend our motion as it saw fit.
As I understand the rules, Your Honour is perfectly correct that basically we cannot amend away the whole thrust of the motion. That is what the New Democratic Party is proposing, and I think members of the NDP must at least restrict their amendment in such a way as to agree with some of the points in our motion before they propose to amend it virtually out of existence, as is the case now. In short, if they do not like our motion, they will have an opportunity to vote against it in due course; but in the meantime they may not amend it to such an extent that they automatically defeat our motion with their amendment.

Mr. Speaker, it is both obvious and true that we have been doing quite a bit of drafting this afternoon. First we had to draft a subamendment to the amendment which was first moved by the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens). Then, we had to redraft that to fit the suggested change proposed by the Chair. Then, with about 30 seconds' notice, another amendment was submitted

by the hon. member for York-Simcoe, and we had to try to fit into that.
1 do not ask for any concession because of that, but that is part of the picture. However, I point out in answer to what the hon. member for York-Simcoe just said that his is a motion which is critical of the budget. In fact, it rejects the budget because it increases the deficit without providing a genuine economic stimulus. We accept that, but we qualify the reasons for our rejecting the budget and make other suggestions as to how to do something about it.
It is perfectly true that a subamendment has to be relevant to the amendment. The amendment deals with the budget and its faults and proposes something in its place. I suggest that in our subamendment we are accepting the rejection of the budget. We are qualifying or altering the reasons for that rejection, but it seems to me that it is in the same ball park. It is in the regulations that a subamendment must be relevant to the amendment, and I hope we do not have to have another hour's debate on procedure.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the subamendment may be in the same league, but I have to agree with the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) that it is certainly not in the same ball park nor part of the same ball game. I have always emulated and admired the example set by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) in supporting the Chair on every possible occasion. I think he saw fit to support the Chair when my amendment was under consideration. The amendment moved by my colleague, the hon. member for York-Simcoe, is under consideration now, and I must say that I hope the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre will find it equally admirable of me if I support the Chair in the reservations Your Honour expressed regarding this subamendment.
I think the hon. member for York-Simcoe is quite correct in saying that one cannot amend away the whole thrust of an amendment. For whatever reason, I think that is what is being attempted here, and I am sure that given a few moments and given the drafting skill of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, which is revered in every parliament in the Commonwealth, he will be able to come up with an amendment which will satisfy the Chair, the government-which will have the right to vote-and also satisfy us as to its procedural acceptability. If the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre needs a little time, we are, of course, prepared to give it to him.
It would be easier if the government would review its budget.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, surely no one has any objection to your taking all the time required to give a ruling on whether or not the subamendment is receivable. What strikes one, however, is how difficult it is for the opposition parties to criticize legitimately the budget brought down by the government. Which leads one to wonder what they would do if they were on this side of the House. Mr. Speaker, I suggest we resume the
November 17, 1978

debate. We have, on this side of the House, several hon. members who are willing and ready, to say the least, to praise last night's fine budget. We shall await your ruling at your leisure on the subamendment of the New Democratic Party.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I hesitate to accept the suggestion of the parliamentary secretary because it might bring about the same problem and at the same time work against one of the parties in the House who has a priority at this time, under the practices of this House, to present a subamendment.
If I were to come to the Chair on Monday and make a negative ruling on this subamendment, at whatever time, that might preclude a representative of the New Democratic Party from exercising his right to move another subamendment. 1 wonder if the House would be prepared at this time to accept my suggestion that I reserve the right of a representative of the New Democratic Party to move another submendment. I base my suggestion on the fact that I am quite concerned about the wording of this subamendment. Perhaps its objective might not go against the rules of the House if it were worded in another way or attached to the amendment in another way. So without ruling out the content of the motion, I find fault with the way it is attached to the amendment. At the same time, I am ready to protect the right of the hon. member's party to have one of his colleagues move another amendment on Monday.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am prepared to agree to allow the NDP to put an amendment in an appropriate way, as you suggested, or in some other way that we could work out. However that is done, we are certainly prepared to agree to that.
[ Translation]

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Of course, Mr. Speaker, we are willing to help the opposition in its efforts to adjust to the rules of the House.

Yes, Mr. Speaker, we are prepared to accept that. I was trying to draft something fast, but it would make more sense for us to present a new motion on Monday. But I take it that if the House agrees now to what is proposed, the Chair will not accept a subamendment from anyone else until another New Democratic Party member gets the floor.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is that agreed and so ordered?
Agreed.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
For the information of hon. members, the House agrees to reserve the right of another member of the New Democratic Party to introduce an amendment to the amendment moved by the official opposition and the Chair will then decide whether that amendment is in order. At this time I consider that even if the amendment to the amendment
The Budget-Mr. Saltsman moved by the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman) might not be contrary to our standing orders and our practices, the manner in which it is proposed and related to the proposal of the official opposition seems to me entirely out of order and thus goes beyond the substance of the main motion and at the same time, I think, gives rise to a new proposal which replaces part of the one already made by the official opposition.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there has been some consultation among the parties with respect to the debate. It had to do with the divisions that will be taken. In fact, announcements were made by the government House leader on the time of the vote when he answered questions on the business of the House yesterday. I would just like it to be understood that in terms of the consent we are giving to accommodate reasonably the dilemma in which we find ourselves, we can take it that today is the first day of the budget debate. I want to make sure there is no doubt in my friend's mind about that.
That is quite clear.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: And it is understood that the second day will be Monday, and that there will be a vote on that amendment on Monday evening, assuming an appropriate amendment is put by my friend or his colleague; and that the debate will carry on, not as I had agreed, but as the government House leader has indicated and in accordance with the plans of the government for the balance of the week.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I rely on the statement made by the Deputy Prime Minister yesterday. I think it is obvious that we have to act accordingly.

But there might be an interruption. Should that not be made clear? The hon. member for Grenville-Carleton is speaking as though the debate would go on every day next week. I think there was a reservation regarding the possibility of one day's interruption.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: When I said I would rely on the statement made by the government House leader, it included that possibility, of course.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: To make sure that this is clear, let me ask whether that possibility could not arise on Monday.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, that was not specified. I still have to rely on the statement made by the Deputy Prime Minister. If anything is to change before Monday, of course the House leaders of the other parties will be informed in advance.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
On the second day of the budget debate, the Chair will ensure that a member of the NDP seeking the floor will be recognized for the purpose of presenting a subamendment.

November 17, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Laprise

Mr. Speaker, we found ourselves in some confusion probably because there was confusion as well in the speech on the budget itself last night. Such problems of "adjusting" to move amendments or subamendments as we were just faced with a while ago makes us smile because generally we never had much problems to devise appropriate amendments and I could hardly comment on that amendment or subamendment because so many have been tabled. Still I can at least speak on the intent of the amendment and subamendment since the latter was preceeded by a speech.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the amendment proposed by the representative of the Progessive Conservative party, the official opposition, calls for a lower deficit and economic incentives. Well, Mr. Speaker, we can only approve strongly such an amendment. Elowever, the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) did not tell us what the Conservative party would do if it were in power to lower the considerable deficit we have known for years. And knowing the monetary policy of the Conservative party, which is more or less the same as that of the Liberal party, I think they will have much difficulty devising ways of cutting down those deficits while at the same time improving the Canadian economy since they follow the same monetary policy.
Mr. Speaker, earlier I heard the hon. member for York-Simcoe criticize this administration. He was right on nearly everything, but as I was listening to him I wondered what would have happened if since 1968 for example, he had been on the other side of the House? Undoubtedly, Mr. Speaker, we would have had roughly the same difficulties. The Progressive Conservative party is undoubtedly full of good intentions but the administration it gave us when it was in office in the late fifties and early sixties shows that in terms of administration they are not much more capable than the Liberal administration has been since 1963. During the Progessive Conservative administration we had a period of terrible unemployment, the dollar went down, we had a period of intense inflation, and that is in part practically what caused the Progressive Conservative party to be defeated in 1962-63. So today, Mr. Speaker, they want to replace the Liberal party but with the same means to administer this country. Mr. Speaker, the same causes have the same effects. So as far as I am concerned 1 do not have any more confidence in the policies of the Progessive Conservative party than I have in the Liberal party currently in office.
I listened also to the arguments of the hon. member of the New Democratic Party, the hon. member for Waterloo-Cam-bridge (Mr. Saltsman), and he was practically at the opposite of what the representative of the Conservative party proposed. For the representative of the New Democratic Party, public projects should be increased substantially to fight unemployment. Fighting unemployment, Mr. Speaker, would be a good

idea but increasing public projects in the sense that was suggested means increasing the current government deficit.
Mr. Speaker, that deficit is considerable and has become a frightening plague for the taxpayers of this country. Since 1975-and that is only three years ago-the public debt in Canada has doubled. If you take the budget deficit of 1977-78 and 1978-79 and the forecast for 1979-80 you get a total deficit of $31.12 billion. Mr. Speaker, administering like that when you have a Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) coming out with estimates like that, you do not have to be a genius to administer with debts like that. Anyone, Mr. Speaker, could do it, but administering a country soundly and running a country like the people want it to be run is another thing. I believe that what we have now on the government side is an incapacity to do so. The Minister of Finance might be well intentioned but last night he was unable to introduce a budget to revive the Canadian economy which is in great difficulty, he was unable to introduce a budget to reduce the rate of unemployment in Canada, he was unable to introduce a budget to reduce substantially the cost of living we now have in Canada. Of course, Mr. Speaker, the margin of the Minister of Finance is very narrow, I would say almost nonexisting, because of huge expenses which are far higher than revenues. And the government can hardly get more from income tax than it already does, because Canadian taxpayers are overtaxed as it is. They cannot afford to pay more. And today our workers, those who have a job, are overburdened. They must pay for about 50 per cent of the Canadian people and they account for an ever decreasing percentage of the labour market. They must pay for just about all those who do not work for one reason or another. They have to support all those people and the entire government machinery.
Some workers are beginning to wonder whether it is more advantageous to be outside the labour market rather than being at work. More and more people are worrying about that. The gap between the poor and the rich grows wider and wider, and it is increasingly difficult for the middle class to live under such an administration. So, Mr. Speaker, a lot of criticism can be levelled at the government that has been in power for the past ten years, at least with regard to the present administration and it has been done in all sorts of ways and I do not intend this afternoon to come back on this kind of criticism. I would rather spend a few minutes trying to make the House of Commons and the Canadian people understand that we must get off the beaten path, that we must forgo this system which is leading Canada to bankruptcy.
We have come to the point, Mr. Speaker, where the interest on the national debt this year is as large as the Canadian government's budget in 1962, a date which is not so remote after all. One is entitled to wonder in what kind of a situation we find ourselves and when we are talking about billions of dollars we are not dealing with peanuts. These are billions of
November 17, 1978

dollars which we are giving away every year. We have now gone over the $6.5 billion mark in interests on the national debt and these $6.5 billion are not recycled within the government. When we tax workers to pay for old age security pensions, family allowances and the cost of public works, development projects of all kinds, all that money eventually finds its way back to the government somehow. But when we tax the same workers to pay the interest on the monumental debt of our country to those who have a claim to that debt, all that money is not redistributed, it has to be borrowed again at current annual interest rates which have now reached 10 per cent.
Mr. Speaker, Canadians have the right and are beginning to wonder where all this will lead us. What will the situation be next year? What will it be in two years? This cannot last forever, there will be a breakdown somewhere, sometime. We have had the 1939 crash and we undoubtedly find ourselves on the eve of another one because there are limits to the level of indebtedness of a country and its people. In the thirties, when the crisis took place, which was called then an economic crisis, nobody had any money. There was a surplus a goods everywhere which people did not know what to do with, the stores were stacked up with all kinds of commodities. There were unemployed people everywhere eager to work but there was no employment for them and those worked were not getting paid.
Then, Mr. Speaker, people were suffering in the midst of abundance. When war was declared, suddenly we could find the money that was lacking a few months before. However, tractors, had to be built to make war, machines had to be built, ammunitions were needed and there was work for everybody. The necessary money was found. And as men were workig in factories producing war equipment and ammunitions, salaries were paid and wage earners were buying consumer goods which in term gave work to other people so that during the war everybody was working, any disabled man could find a job; in fact, everybody was working. Such was wartime economy. But no sooner had the hostilities come to an end, that we found ourselves in the same predicament. We were having economic and financial problems and the government, in an attempt to save the economy and preserve jobs, sank ever deeper into debt.
Mr. Speaker, surely it is easy to find an alternative to such an administration, and other means must be looked for, other than those we know and other than those proposed by current economists.
We are laughed at on occasion. When I heard the minister making his speech, I remember the sixties when the same minister was making jokes at the Caouette dollar, the Social Credit dollar. He found that funny. But today we have Chretien's 85 cents, and this is not much funnier. Social Credit monetary proposals were then called "funny money." Today we have sad money and it hurts even though the minister repeatedly suggested last summer, that the Canadian dollar devaluation was something that could enhance the economy,
The Budget-Mr. Laprise
would promote exports. Mr. Speaker, rather than trying to export our production, developing an international market, let us try rather to develop a domestic market, a home market by giving back our Canadian dollar its purchasing power, the real value it has lost because of this administration.
That is what he should try: The Minister of Finance stated that the 90, 89, 88 cents and even 85 cents, and it went down to 84 cents, that dollar made for cheaper exports. We could export more. But last night the minister of Finance told us the opposite in his budget. This is what I find on page 5, and I quote:
The consumer price index rose more sharply than has been expected.
He erred across the board, this is nothing new.
In September, it was 8.6 per cent higher then a year earlier. This renewed outburst of inflation-
Please note this:
This renewed outburst of inflation was not the result of any acceleration in our own incomes or our own domestic costs. It was the result of higher food prices and the decline in the dollar.
Last night the minister agreed that the renewed outburst of inflation was due to the decline in the dollar. This flies in the face of the statements he made during all of last summer, when we questioned him, in the course of the last session and the beginning of the current one, on the Canadian dollar devaluation. If the Canadian dollar devaluation could help our exports and improve the Canadian economic climate, why not lower it to 83 cents, 75 cents and even 50 cents if this is effective?
The proof is that the minister did not believe it at all since, along with the governor of the Bank of Canada, they made every effort to borrow on the American market and elsewhere in an attempt to save the dollar. Each time it was exactly the opposite that should have been done. All they did in fact was to devise a means of exporting interests and dividends, of exporting and increasing the flow of our money out of the country, when it should have been kept here.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the government has only three means of obtaining the funds needed to meet its obligations, and for the government, the main obligation is to provide an efficient administration to the entire population, not only to parts of it but to the entire population. That is why it must offer advantages not only to big owners of what I would call chicken coops, but also to owners of single family dwellings, not only to big owners but to small owners as well. That was omitted in the budget speech we heard last night. There is nothing there for the small homeowner or the tenant who wants to buy a home, they were completely disregarded. Now, Mr. Speaker, this is one of the government's obligations.
Small and medium-sized businesses were also largely overlooked. Nothing new was done in addition to what we already have, and the government is only starting to show concern for small and medium-sized businesses. Yet we know how much

November 17, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Laprise
this type of business generates jobs. Therefore, much more should be done in that direction, but there was nothing in the budget speech which was far more noteworthy by its omissions than by its content. Also, Mr. Speaker, the government has the obligation to ensure a decent standard of living to the people of Canada. At present, 20 per cent to 25 per cent of the population is living below the poverty line, especially the senior citizens of Canada. There are disabled, sick and socially handicapped people who are without jobs and there are others who do have a job but who work for the minimum wages allowed by the provincial governments. Mr. Speaker, almost 25 per cent of our population live below the poverty line. As a matter of fact, somebody mentioned today that the poverty line for a family of four was $11,000 a year. Mr. Speaker, many families live on a much smaller income. It is the government's responsibility to take care of them.
Mr. Speaker, in order to obtain the necessary funds to meet its obligations, the government can levy taxes-and we know it does not hesitate to do so. It has the authority to tax citizens and corporations alike, to take the money out of their pockets. Last night, while I was listening to the minister's budget speech in the House, I noted the tax cut offered to the Canadian people. I noted the 9 per cent tax credit or indexation of the personal income tax and true, I felt relieved for the Canadian workers, but the government has nothing to lose by granting this indexation.
In the tables which were tabled before us last night in the budget speech and which have been included in Hansard we can see in Table 2-Forecast for 1979-80-under personal income tax that despite a supplementary indexation of 9 per cent the government is going to collect an additional $1.85 billion. The minister can always brag about his allowing for a fiscal reduction; in fact because of the wage increase that almost all workers get during the year, the government will get an ever increasing tax amount but it will not be seen as such by the people.
Mr. Speaker, when the minister proposes to reduce the sales tax from 12 per cent down to 9 per cent, he plays the same trick once again, since prices and costs increase, the government is able to get more money through the taxes on manufactured items. The government does not lose anything in this 3 per cent reduction, even though we hope the consumer will draw some kind of advantage out of it in the end. Mr. Speaker, the government can get money through taxes and we know how it uses it.
Here is another way: the government could borrow from the people, from institutions and corporations and pay back the money it has borrowed. But the government almost never pays these sums back, it pays only the interest. When Canada Savings Bonds fall due, the government makes every effort to convince the buyers to keep them for another term. The

government offers higher interest rates in the hope that bond owners will renew them. But if the owners want their money, the government must borrow to pay them. Then it is like digging a hole to fill another one, but at the end we are still left with a hole.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the second system the government is using to get funds for its administration.
The third system the government may use to get funds and which they do not want to resort to is simply to create money and spend the funds thus created for public projects. That is the very third power of the government which could change completely the administration of the country and restore a sound administration which Canadians call for and are entitled to expect.
Mr. Speaker, the government refuses to exercise that third option because its masters, those who control it behind the curtains, that occult power which nobody knows, nobody sees, forbid the government to exercise that third option.
In 1977, my colleague from Richmond (Mr. Beaudoin) asked the Minister of Finance a question which I shall repeat here for your information, Mr. Speaker, and that of hon. members. I quote:
-this misunderstanding between the federal government and the province of Quebec depends mostly on the fact that we have economic problems; since money is manmade, why does the Minister of Finance not urge the Bank of Canada to open a new credit for the federal government, in co-operation with the provinces, to promote or Finance new public projects in municipalities and school boards in order to deal with unemployment and create new jobs?
Well, Mr. Speaker, here is the answer of the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Finance of the present Liberal government, and I quote:
The Canadian monetary policy is well known and it has been formulated by the governor of the Bank of Canada and I do not intend to ask him to change his policy.
Then, Mr. Speaker, who is governing the country? Is it the Minister of Finance elected by Canadians or the governor of the Bank of Canada who is only known by 1 per cent of Canadians because nobody votes for him? And yet he is the man who administers our financial policy in Canada. He is in the driver's seat but answerable to nobody. Mr. Speaker, such conditions cannot go on. The present minister or the next one, this government or the next one will have to assume their responsibilities. They have to assume the responsibilities entrusted by the people and instruct the Bank of Canada to do what they have to do. At the present time, it is the tail that makes the dog wag and not the other way around; everything is mixed up. We have to put back some order and put things as they should be. The Minister of Finance did not say that in his budget speech yesterday and the spokesmen for the Progressive Conservative party and the New Democratic Party avoided making such proposals. They have good intentions, but they did not suggest any measure to do something. We should remove those who are not qualified to manage our economy
November 17, 1978

and give that responsibility to the people's representatives elected by the people. They are the ones who should assume that responsibility.

speakeroldname: Hon. A. C. Abbott (Minister of State (Small Business)):
speechtext:
As
the first supporter of the government speaking on the budget, Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) for what he has produced in what are agreed to be very difficult circumstances. The minister has come up with a prudent, responsible and equitable budget which goes a long way to both stimulating the economy and also showing the national and international community that the government is wholly responsible in its position today and in the circumstances that limit it. I think that the responsible comment in the press tends to confirm this fact.
The official critic for the opposition, the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens), spoke, I think somewhat irresponsibly, on a number of issues and failed to a large extent to come to grips with some of the real benefits and concerns in the budget. He gave a very lengthy, gloomy resume of what he saw to be the problems in the economy. He referred to matters like paper clips, floor mats, and his concerns about Petro-Canada, all inaccurate and ominous statements about the national state of the economy; but he is filled with hope that there will be a Tory government in 1979.
I believe it was Samuel Johnson who said that if a person marries for a second time, it is the triumph of hope over experience. Every now and then I think that the public mind tends to forget the years under Tory governments. Mercifully we have not had too many of them, but those we have had are a very sharp reminder to any who have experienced the mismanagement, irresponsibility and reactionary character which they have imposed. Whether it was R. B. Bennett or the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), they were dismal and hapless performances.
When the hon. member for York-Simcoe speaks of his high hopes for the Clark government, as he refers to it, I suggest that these hopes are perhaps excessive or optimistic. As hon. members may be aware, 1979 has been designated by the United Nations to be the International Year of the Child, but I do not think that members opposite should hope that it will be the year of a Clark government. I do not think that the International Year of the Child should be taken as an automatic assumption that we will have a Clark government.
Listening to the hon. member for York-Simcoe last night and today would suggest to any new arrival to this parliament or to the country who was listening to his speech that Canada has had a deplorable ten years economically and is on the verge of financial collapse. All the facts, however, are contrary to that statement, and these facts have been stated both by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Finance, who last night, for instance, stated that in this past year
362,000	more Canadians were employed and that our exports reached an all-time high.
The Budget-Mr. Abbott
A recent report of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) on the annual survey of the capital intentions of the large industries in Canada shows that there is going to be a very distinct strengthening in capital intentions. In other words, all the measures and indices that are currently revealing themselves show that, far from the economy being in the depressed and deplorable state that the hon. member would try to convince the Canadian people it is in, in reality it is showing real signs of improvement. The record of the past ten years has been considerably brighter than he would suggest.
One need only refer to the statistics supplied by the OECD to confirm this. They show, for instance, that the rate of growth in the labour force in Canada between 1968 and 1977 was the highest of all member countries. The cost of living index for 1978 showed the United States had the smallest increase, Canada was second, then came West Germany, Sweden, Switzerland, Belgium, Denmark-countries that the hon. member tried to suggest last night and today had done much better than Canada. Food prices are shown as being the least costly in Canada in 1978, with the United States coming second. The rate of growth in real domestic product between 1968 and 1977 showed Canada first. There is much talk about the need for greater stimulus through their regrettable tax proposal in the area of housing starts, yet Canada is listed second amongst the countries from 1972 to 1977. Belgium came first and the United States third.
It is one thing for hon. members opposite to engage in the cut and thrust of parliamentary debate, one thing for them to try to fool themselves. But I suggest that at a time when a lot of Canadians are looking for leadership from parliament, and are expecting some degree of responsibility, for the official financial critic of the official opposition to try to cast such a spurious pall of pessimism across the Canadian scene, suggesting that our economy is in a shambles, does no credit to him, to his party or to his country.
I should like to touch on some aspects of the budget itself for a few minutes, Mr. Speaker, and on some things other budgets in the recent past have provided in the area of small business. The hon. member who last spoke suggested that nothing was done for small business in this budget. I would point out that the provisions relating to development and the increase in the employment allowance are two notable features which mean a great deal to small business people. These come on the heels of recent changes which have given support to small business.
In the provision for the reduction of the manufacturing tax from 12 per cent to 9 per cent, it should be remembered that
8,000	of the 9,000 members of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association are involved in small business. The vast number of manufacturers in Canada fall into this category. The reduction of this tax will not only stimulate big industry but will have a marked impact on the prosperity of industry as a whole in Canada in which small business is dominant.

The Budget-Mr. Abbott
The pattern in tax policies that now exists in Canada for small business has cut a wide swath. I reminded hon. members before of the very real accomplishments of the government. We have a tax system for small business which is more favourable than that of any other country in the world.
I do not say this, as the hon. member for York Simcoe would, simply because I want to say it or hear it said, and hope somebody is going to believe it. I say it because other commentators, such as Mr. John Bulloch, president of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, say it. The report that was issued by the Minister of Finance last night gives a careful study of the comparative tax systems of the United States. The hon. member for York-Simcoe tried to assert theirs was so much more beneficial than Canada's but he had not read the report.
The report states it is evident that the Canadian system is considerably more generous than the United States system. Canada extends the low rate of a significantly larger amount of small business income and does not impose any special penalties on the sheltering of business income in the corporate entity, it points out. The report also says that the combined corporation and personal tax burden on corporation income is much lower in Canada than in the United States due to the presence of the dividend tax credit. It says that the credit causes the combined corporation and personal taxes on small business income to be even lower than the personal tax on, say, wages and salaries.
When you consider the special tax rate for small business which results in some 20 per cent or 21 per cent less tax being paid than is paid by larger companies, and add to that the recent tax change whereby family businesses have been provided with roll-over provisions so that intergenerational transfers can take place without the application of the capital gains tax, when you consider the elimination of the sales tax payable by small businesses representing 20 per cent of all the manufacturers in Canada, with almost 50 per cent of them being eligible for a much reduced filing of returns system, when you remind yourself that as of last spring we have had a far more liberal provision for write-offs of losses against other income, then I think I can say with confidence, without going into a number of other measures which have been passed by the government to help small business in the way of tax reform, that it amply substantiates my point that this government has set its sights on small business and has helped them to an extent that no other country in the world can demonstrate in the area of taxation.
I think as the member of parliament for Mississauga, an area in the industrial heartland of Ontario, I should point out that the greatest job-creation vehicle, the greatest engine for economic growth, is the manufacturing sector. I was very pleased that the Minister of Finance addressed this area and provided relief in the form of a reduction in the manufacturers' sales tax so that this important sector will receive the stimulus it needs to generate the sort of jobs we need in Canada.
I should like to say something about the accusations concerning the Petro-Canada transaction. I think it is unfortunate

November 17, 1978
that the hon. member for York-Simcoe attempted to cast doubts on the merits of this proposal. Of course, he was an active member of the energy committee. Many of us who sat on that committee remember his dogged opposition and his attempt to filibuster passage of the bill. From the inception of the idea of Petro-Can it was said that, apart from the United States, no other western industrial country lacked a government oil company. British Petroleum belonged to the British government, the French government owned a company, the German government had a company. All these government-owned companies act as a balance-a player at the table in their country's national strategies to counteract the overwhelming influence of the great international oil companies that are dominant elsewhere. Canada is particularly vulnerable as a major oil producer where all the major oil companies doing business have been foreign dominated, foreign owned and foreign managed. When I say the United States is an exception, it must be remembered that three or four of the largest oil concerns in the world are based in the United States, which has a very real interest or control over their policies. Canada lacked this.
Today, by virtue of this transaction, Petro-Can if fulfilling the mandate it was given, which is to equip itself to be a player at the table and thus provide a kind of balance against the policies of the major oil companies. The suggestions made by the hon. member for York-Simcoe that a vast new debt is being placed on the shoulders of the Canadian taxpayer, when the reverse is true, is a misleading comment. Whether it was deliberate or not, I am not prepared to say. It is well known that Petro-Canada is financing the acquisition through banking sources of its own negotiations. The payment of these loans will be paid out of cash flow from the combined assets of the two companies, amounting to some $232 million annually. The banks that have assisted in financing this acquisition have done so with hard-headed realism because these loans are not being guaranteed by the federal government, which is the advice I have.
Therefore, I suggest his representations that somehow the Canadian taxpayer is having money extracted from him that should otherwise be put into homes or into other forms of activity in Canada is entirely misleading. I suggest it should be revealed as such and the hon. member should rise in his place and point out to the Canadian people, through parliament, the inaccuracy of his statement.
The hon. member's anxiety to show up the malevolence of Crown corporations as he sees it was revealed in his condemnation of the Export Development Corporation. Here is a corporation that has never had a loss. It consistently earns a profit, it has created thousands of jobs in Canada for foreign projects and has insured projects by Canadians. It has seen hundreds of millions of dollars invested at no cost to the Canadian taxpayer, and it has given great opportunities to Canadian manufacturers. Yet the hon. member and others over there say the policy of the Export Development Corporation is to export Canadian jobs, somehow trying to suggest that

November 17, 1978

there are projects abroad that, if Canada does not agree to do them, will not get done.
By using these red herrings, and by making them a large part of his condemnation of the very responsible budget that was delivered last night, the hon. member has shown the bankruptcy of his own ideas and that he is incapable of meaningful criticism. The hon. member is filled with hopes for a Clark government. Some of us, however, were struck by the inability of himself and his colleagues to draft even their motion in opposition, with the result that we had to take valuable time to straighten up what should surely have been a simple task, and not recite again what parliament had seen fit to dispose of previously.
I would like to turn to the question of mortgage interest deductions. This is a subject that we are going to hear a great deal more about. I think there is a real misunderstanding among a lot of people as to what should constitute an equitable tax system. I was reading a comment the other day in an American paper on tax policy. The question of tax in the American system was discussed. It spoke of the "three martini lunch". I know that the hon. member for York-Simcoe is a man of abstemious habits and I certainly would not accuse him of having a three-martini lunch, although the content of his speech would seem to indicate some blurring of ideas.
The three-martini lunch, the expense account lunch, was one element in the ability of people with large incomes to treat themselves to rich meals on a daily basis and write them off against income tax in a way that citizens of poorer status cannot do. This is greatly resented by many people who hear about expense accounts. I do not suggest there are many business people in Canada who take advantage of this type of tax deduction.
The American system also provides for donations to museums or art galleries by people in very high income tax brackets. They are able to take the entire donation and write it off against their taxes. While indeed the art gallery may be the beneficiary, frequently people in the 75 per cent tax bracket are able to create for themselves a very substantial tax relief in a way that is not available to ordinary citizens. The esteem of such individuals is raised in the eyes of the community and the art gallery benefits. Nonetheless, it is a deduction from income tax revenue which must be raised in other ways from somebody else. Therefore, the burden falls on those who do not have the means to contribute to such charities.
Then there is the deduction the Americans have for municipal tax free bonds. Again, the municipalities are the beneficiaries. They get money which is invested by wealthy people in high income brackets who then get tax-free income from these tax-free municipal bonds. Nonetheless, the fact that those taxes are not received by the federal government from these wealthy citizens means that the over-all tax has to be higher. I suggest once again there is something basically inequitable about that deduction.
The United States allows for what hon. members opposite have been advocating for the last few weeks, that is, the deduction of mortgage interest and municipal taxes. Who is
The Budget-Mr. Abbott
entitled to enjoy this benefit? People obviously who have initial capital to invest in real property in homes, and people who are paying municipal taxes. What of the ederly people who have already paid their mortgages off and have spent their lives doing so? Out of their modest income they must pay the full tax without such a reduction for mortgage interest. What of the poorer people who, by necessity, remain tenants? There must be a growing number of them due to the high cost of buying a home. They must watch while those who enjoy home ownership and a larger income deduct the interest on their mortgage payments from their income. So again, what are the consequences? Some people get a benefit and others do not, and the over-all rates of taxation must be higher so that the system as a whole may raise the tax revenues needed.
The Tory idea sounds good and it sounds as though it will create a lot of new housing. The fact is, if you trace these kinds of deductions you see they are essentially inequitable. If we have this kind of inequity in a tax system where poorer people on modest incomes see people across the street enjoying rich expense account living, making handsome donations to art galleries and writing them off against their taxes, buying tax free bonds or deducting all their mortgage interest or municipal taxes, somehow there will be a massive number of people in this country who will say: "Our basic tax system is unfair, I have no respect for it, and consequently I have no respect for the government that imposes it."
I suggest it is not enough for an opposition, loyal or otherwise, to come forward with measures which would create growing inequity in our taxation system. The Minister of Finance last night produced a budget which maintained a consistent attitude toward this whole question of equity. Some commentators in their wisdom criticized it as a business budget without noting the number of measures which took away certain of the advantages business has been getting, such as the loophole provision for debentures and preferred stock being classified as equity instruments whereas they are really debt instruments. This is one area where business will have to pay more for its borrowing.
The budget as a whole leaned toward the creation of tax relief. Consumers will benefit from the reduction in the tax on manufactured goods. Also, we have built into the system the indexation of taxes so that where there is an increase in the cost of living citizens will enjoy some protection. There is also the raising of the exemption so that families pay less tax when costs are higher.
I simply wish to reiterate that while the economy is not as strong as we would wish it to be, and while there are great ills afoot in this country and in the world, I consider that the Minister of Finance has approached his very difficult task- and let no one doubt that he has on his shoulders as heavy a burden of responsibility as any minister of finance in the history of this country-with optimism, with intelligence, with courage, with prudence and with wisdom.

November 17, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Abbott
We in this country often feel that it is open season on all politicians and that they can be criticized at will. That is fair game. But I do think it is irresponsible for an opposition, which for some reason or other is now dreaming ever more positively that it will form a government, to cast such doubt upon the economy as to lower the self-esteem of the Canadian people and their standing in the eyes of the world. I believe that in the months ahead the revitalizing of the economy, the renewed growth of our industry taking advantage of the lower rate of the Canadian dollar, the increasing productivity of the workers, the increased trade opportunities and the stimulation afforded by this budget, will enable us to show that the government and the Minister of Finance have rendered Canada very effective service in the budget which has been brought down.
I do not know whether it is possible to call it five o'clock, Mr. Speaker, but if it is I would so recommend.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Is it agreed we call it five o'clock?

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: I think the minister has used his time. With all due respect, perhaps I might call it five o'clock.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Hon. members have heard the suggestion that we call it five o'clock. Is that agreed?
I was prepared to call it five o'clock but I do have one or two more comments to make and if it is not five o'clock I had better carry on.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The minister still has two minutes in which to conclude his remarks. Does he have consent to conclude his remarks?

I presume that if I do have two minutes left I do not need the indulgence of the House to use them. I am sorry the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) has only just arrived. I had hoped he would have listened, a chastened figure, to what I had to say, but he is a busy man and will have to read my remarks. I would have liked him to be here, though. I heard him on television explaining his position on mortgage deductions and it did not seem to me he was quite clear about it. I do not know how much time he has spent reviewing the experience in the United States, but no doubt at a later stage he will want to consider whether his proposal is as responsible as he thinks it is at the present time.
Last night, when we talked about the inequity of certain people not being homeowners and thus not being in a position to take advantage of a mortgage allowance, the hon. member for York-Simcoe gave us the impression that somehow, just because some people are tenants and want to become homeowners, the problem is corrected.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I have to interrupt the hon. gentleman. His allotted time has expired.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: As I indicated a while ago, Mr. Speaker, I will now call it five o'clock. 1 know the Leader of the Opposition has a very strong stomach but I doubt he could stand reading the drivel we have been hearing for the last while.
It is five o'clock anyway.
